claim: CarD is an essential activator in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: CarD, an essential activator in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is found in many bacteria, including Thermus species, but absent in Escherichia coli.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in this manuscript, but references prior work.

claim: CarD is found in many bacteria, including Thermus species.
source: CarD, an essential activator in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is found in many bacteria, including Thermus species, but absent in Escherichia coli.
evidence: Supported by Table 1 showing distribution of CarD across bacterial phyla.

claim: CarD is absent in Escherichia coli.
source: CarD, an essential activator in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is found in many bacteria, including Thermus species, but absent in Escherichia coli.
evidence: Supported by Table 1 showing CarD absence in Proteobacteria-γ (which includes Escherichia).

claim: CarD interacts with the unique DNA topology presented by the upstream double-stranded/single-stranded DNA junction of the transcription bubble.
source: The structures show CarD interacts with the unique DNA topology presented by the upstream double-stranded/single-stranded DNA junction of the transcription bubble.
evidence: Supported by crystal structures shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: A conserved CarD Trp residue serves as a minor groove wedge, preventing collapse of the transcription bubble to stabilize the transcription initiation complex.
source: We confirm that our structures correspond to functional activation complexes, and extend our understanding of the role of a conserved CarD Trp residue that serves as a minor groove wedge, preventing collapse of the transcription bubble to stabilize the transcription initiation complex.
evidence: Supported by structural data in Figure 2 and functional assays in Figures 3, 5, and 6.

claim: Many bacterial RNAPs form unstable promoter complexes, explaining the need for CarD.
source: Unlike E. coli RNAP, many bacterial RNAPs form unstable promoter complexes, explaining the need for CarD.
evidence: Supported by half-life measurements in Figure 5 showing Thermus RNAP forms less stable complexes than E. coli RNAP.

claim: σ factors direct the catalytic core of the RNA polymerase to promoter DNA sites.
source: First, dissociable promoter specificity subunits, σ factors, direct the catalytic core of the RNA polymerase (RNAP) to promoter DNA sites and play a key role in unwinding the DNA duplex to create the transcription bubble in the RNAP holoenzyme open promoter complex (RPo) (Feklistov et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Feklistov et al., 2014).

claim: σ factors play a key role in unwinding the DNA duplex to create the transcription bubble in the RNAP holoenzyme open promoter complex.
source: First, dissociable promoter specificity subunits, σ factors, direct the catalytic core of the RNA polymerase (RNAP) to promoter DNA sites and play a key role in unwinding the DNA duplex to create the transcription bubble in the RNAP holoenzyme open promoter complex (RPo) (Feklistov et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Feklistov et al., 2014).

claim: The majority of transcription activators characterized to date are dimeric proteins that bind operators upstream of the promoter −35 element.
source: The majority of transcription activators characterized to date are dimeric proteins that bind operators upstream of the promoter −35 element and directly contact the RNAP α subunit (Ebright, 1993), the σ4 domain positioned at the −35 element, or both (Nickels et al., 2002; Dove et al., 2003; Jain et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Ebright, 1993; Nickels et al., 2002; Dove et al., 2003; Jain et al., 2004).

claim: CarD was first identified as a regulator of ribosomal RNA transcription in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: CarD, first identified as a regulator of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) transcription in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), is a transcriptional activator widely distributed among bacterial species, including Thermus species (Stallings et al., 2009; Srivastava et al., 2013), but is absent in Eco (Table 1).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Stallings et al., 2009).

claim: CarD is a global regulator.
source: CarD is a global regulator (Srivastava et al., 2013) that is an essential protein in Mtb (Stallings et al., 2009), the causative agent of tuberculosis.
evidence: Cited from prior work (Srivastava et al., 2013).

claim: CarD is an essential protein in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: CarD is a global regulator (Srivastava et al., 2013) that is an essential protein in Mtb (Stallings et al., 2009), the causative agent of tuberculosis.
evidence: Cited from prior work (Stallings et al., 2009).

claim: Crystal structures of Tth and Mtb CarD reveal an N-terminal domain with a Tudor-like fold (CarD-RID).
source: Crystal structures of Tth (Srivastava et al., 2013) and Mtb (Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013) CarD reveal an N-terminal domain with a Tudor-like fold (CarD-RID, RNAP interacting domain) in common with the Eco transcription repair coupling factor (TRCF)-RID (Deaconescu et al., 2006; Stallings et al., 2009; Weiss et al., 2012), and a helical C-terminal domain (CarD-CTD).
evidence: Cited from prior structural work (Srivastava et al., 2013; Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013).

claim: The CarD-RID interacts with the RNAP β subunit β1-lobe.
source: Unique among known transcription activators, the CarD-RID interacts with the RNAP β subunit β1-lobe (Stallings et al., 2009; Weiss et al., 2012) (corresponding to the eukaryotic RNAP II Rpb2 protrusion domain; Cramer et al., 2001), which is near the upstream portion of the transcription bubble in RPo (Bae et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior work and confirmed by structures in this manuscript (Figures 1, 2).

claim: The RNAP β subunit β1-lobe corresponds to the eukaryotic RNAP II Rpb2 protrusion domain.
source: Unique among known transcription activators, the CarD-RID interacts with the RNAP β subunit β1-lobe (Stallings et al., 2009; Weiss et al., 2012) (corresponding to the eukaryotic RNAP II Rpb2 protrusion domain; Cramer et al., 2001), which is near the upstream portion of the transcription bubble in RPo (Bae et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Cramer et al., 2001).

claim: The disposition of the CarD-CTD with respect to the CarD-RID is widely divergent in Tth and Mtb CarD crystal structures.
source: The disposition of the CarD-CTD with respect to the CarD-RID is widely divergent in Tth and Mtb CarD crystal structures, leading to conflicting models for the CarD activation mechanism (Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013; Srivastava et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior structural work (Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013; Srivastava et al., 2013).

claim: Crystal structures of Thermus aquaticus transcription initiation complexes containing CarD were determined.
source: To resolve these ambiguities, we determined crystal structures of Thermus aquaticus (Taq) transcription initiation complexes (RPo) (Bae et al., 2015) containing CarD (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Reported as experimental results with structures shown in Figures 1 and 2, and crystallographic data in Table 2.

claim: CarD does not alter the transcription bubble.
source: CarD does not alter the transcription bubble.
evidence: Supported by KMnO4 footprinting data in Figure 1D and structural comparison in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The relative orientation of the CarD domains seen in the Thermus CarD structures is only slightly altered in the Thermus CarD/RPo complex.
source: The relative orientation of the CarD domains (CarD-RID, CarD-CTD) seen in the Thermus CarD (Srivastava et al., 2013) and CarD/β1-lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) structures is only slightly altered in the Thermus CarD/RPo complex: the CarD-CTD is rotated ∼11° (with respect to the CarD-RID) to interact with the DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The CarD-CTD is rotated approximately 11° with respect to the CarD-RID to interact with the DNA in the CarD/RPo complex.
source: The relative orientation of the CarD domains (CarD-RID, CarD-CTD) seen in the Thermus CarD (Srivastava et al., 2013) and CarD/β1-lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) structures is only slightly altered in the Thermus CarD/RPo complex: the CarD-CTD is rotated ∼11° (with respect to the CarD-RID) to interact with the DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Binding of the CarD-RID to the RNAP β1-lobe positions the CarD-CTD to interact directly with the upstream ds/ss junction of the transcription bubble.
source: By maintaining the CarD-RID/CTD interface seen in all the Tth CarD structures, binding of the CarD-RID to the RNAP β1-lobe (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) (Stallings et al., 2009; Weiss et al., 2012; Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013) positions the CarD-CTD to interact directly with the upstream ds/ss junction of the transcription bubble (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by crystal structures shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: CarD does not make significant interactions with σA.
source: CarD does not make significant interactions with σA but interacts with the promoter DNA from −14 to −10 from the opposite, (distorted) minor groove side of the DNA (Figure 1A–C) such that the σA/DNA interactions and the structure of the transcription bubble in RPo and CarD/RPo are essentially the same (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: CarD interacts with the promoter DNA from −14 to −10 from the minor groove side of the DNA.
source: CarD does not make significant interactions with σA but interacts with the promoter DNA from −14 to −10 from the opposite, (distorted) minor groove side of the DNA (Figure 1A–C) such that the σA/DNA interactions and the structure of the transcription bubble in RPo and CarD/RPo are essentially the same (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The σA/DNA interactions and the structure of the transcription bubble in RPo and CarD/RPo are essentially the same.
source: CarD does not make significant interactions with σA but interacts with the promoter DNA from −14 to −10 from the opposite, (distorted) minor groove side of the DNA (Figure 1A–C) such that the σA/DNA interactions and the structure of the transcription bubble in RPo and CarD/RPo are essentially the same (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The KMnO4 reactivity of thymine bases within the transcription bubble is identical in the presence or absence of CarD.
source: The KMnO4 reactivity of thymine (T) bases within the transcription bubble (Sasse-Dwight and Gralla, 1991; Ross and Gourse, 2009) is identical in the presence or absence of CarD (Figure 1D, lanes 2 and 3), supporting the structural observation that the transcription bubble is the same with or without CarD.
evidence: Supported by KMnO4 footprinting data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CarD increases the lifetime of RPo.
source: Although CarD does not alter the structure of the transcription bubble, it does increase the lifetime of RPo, as measured by the rate of disappearance of the KMnO4 footprint after challenge with an excess of unlabeled competitor promoter (Figure 1D, lanes 4–7) (Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by KMnO4 footprinting data shown in Figure 1D and cited from prior work (Davis et al., 2015).

claim: The N-terminal ends of two CarD-CTD α-helices (α3 and α5) make direct contacts with the promoter DNA.
source: The N-terminal ends of two CarD-CTD α-helices (α3 and α5) make direct contacts with the promoter DNA (Figure 1C, Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by crystal structures shown in Figures 1C and 2.

claim: The two α-helices are positioned roughly perpendicular to the duplex DNA axis, forming a modest CarD/DNA interaction surface of 380 Å2.
source: The two α-helices are positioned roughly perpendicular to the duplex DNA axis, forming a modest CarD/DNA interaction surface of 380 Å2.
evidence: Calculated from structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: W86 is conserved among greater than 95% of CarD proteins.
source: W86 is conserved among greater than 95% of CarD proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Source code 1) and was shown to be important for CarD function as an activator (Srivastava et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Source code 1.

claim: W86 was shown to be important for CarD function as an activator.
source: W86 is conserved among greater than 95% of CarD proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Source code 1) and was shown to be important for CarD function as an activator (Srivastava et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Srivastava et al., 2013).

claim: The bulky, hydrophobic planar side chain of W86 wedges into the splayed minor groove at the upstream edge of the transcription bubble.
source: The bulky, hydrophobic planar side chain of W86, located at the N-terminal end of α3, wedges into the splayed minor groove at the upstream edge of the transcription bubble (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: CarD-W86 was clearly resolved in electron density maps.
source: Despite the relatively low resolution of our analysis (Table 2), CarD-W86 was clearly resolved in electron density maps (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by electron density maps shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Substitution of the bulky CarD-W86 side chain by Ala greatly reduced the activation efficiency of both Tth and Mtb CarD.
source: Previous work showed that substitution of the bulky CarD-W86 side chain by Ala (Tth CarD-W86A or Mtb CarD-W85A) greatly reduced the activation efficiency of both Tth and Mtb CarD (Srivastava et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Srivastava et al., 2013).

claim: All of the W86 mutants tested showed impaired activity compared to wild-type CarD.
source: All of the mutants tested showed impaired activity compared to wild-type CarD.
evidence: Supported by abortive transcription assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A, F, and Y substitutions of W86 showed partial activation.
source: A, F, and Y substitutions showed partial activation, while substitutions with branched-chain residues (I, L, V) showed no activation (I, V) or even a reduction of transcription compared to wild type CarD (L).
evidence: Supported by abortive transcription assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Substitutions of W86 with branched-chain residues (I, L, V) showed no activation (I, V) or even a reduction of transcription compared to wild type CarD (L).
source: A, F, and Y substitutions showed partial activation, while substitutions with branched-chain residues (I, L, V) showed no activation (I, V) or even a reduction of transcription compared to wild type CarD (L).
evidence: Supported by abortive transcription assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Structural modeling suggests the branched-chain residues would clash with the DNA and interfere with CarD function.
source: Structural modeling suggests the branched-chain residues would clash with the DNA and interfere with CarD function.
evidence: Based on structural modeling using the crystal structure data.

claim: The position of the W86 side chain Nε allows it to interact with T−12(nt) O2.
source: The position of the W86 side chain Nε allows it to interact with T−12(nt) O2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The −12 T/A base pair is a conserved part of the promoter −10 element.
source: The −12 T/A base pair is a conserved part of the promoter −10 element (Shultzaberger et al., 2007), and, as expected, transcription activity from each of the mutant promoters was reduced at least threefold (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Moyle et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Shultzaberger et al., 2007).

claim: Transcription activity from each of the −12 base pair mutant promoters was reduced at least threefold.
source: The −12 T/A base pair is a conserved part of the promoter −10 element (Shultzaberger et al., 2007), and, as expected, transcription activity from each of the mutant promoters was reduced at least threefold (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Moyle et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by abortive transcription assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CarD activation on each mutated −12 promoter was substantially lower than on the wild type promoter.
source: In addition, CarD activation on each mutated promoter was substantially lower than on the wild type promoter (Figure 3B), suggesting that the observed interaction between W86 and T−12(nt) contributes to CarD activity.
evidence: Supported by abortive transcription assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The observed interaction between W86 and T−12(nt) contributes to CarD activity.
source: In addition, CarD activation on each mutated promoter was substantially lower than on the wild type promoter (Figure 3B), suggesting that the observed interaction between W86 and T−12(nt) contributes to CarD activity.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced activation on mutant promoters shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CarD W86F substitution results in an approximately twofold loss in CarD fold activation.
source: Note that the CarD W86F substitution results in an approximately twofold loss in CarD fold activation (Figure 3A, threefold activation for wild-type CarD vs 1.5-fold for W86F), as does substitution of the promoter −12 bp by anything other than the wild-type T/A bp (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The reduced activation efficiency of the CarD-W86F mutant is primarily due to the loss of the minor groove polar interaction with T−12(nt).
source: We tentatively suggest that the reduced activation efficiency of the CarD-W86F mutant is primarily due to the loss of the minor groove polar interaction with T−12(nt).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the data in Figure 3.

claim: A crystal structure of Mtb CarD in complex with an Mtb RNAP β-subunit fragment shows a relative orientation of the CarD-RID/CarD-CTD domains very different from the one in Tth CarD structures.
source: A crystal structure of Mtb CarD in complex with an Mtb RNAP β-subunit fragment that includes the β1-lobe shows a relative orientation of the CarD-RID/CarD-CTD domains very different from the one in our Tth CarD structures, despite high sequence and structural similarity within the domains (Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013; Srivastava et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013; Srivastava et al., 2013).

claim: In the Mtb structure, the CarD-CTD is rotated approximately 140° relative to the CarD-RID.
source: In the Mtb structure, the CarD-CTD is rotated ∼140° relative to the CarD-RID (Figure 4A).
evidence: Cited from prior work and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Structural modeling in the context of RPo positions the Mtb CarD-CTD and the functionally important W85 away from the promoter DNA.
source: Structural modeling in the context of RPo positions the Mtb CarD-CTD and the functionally important W85 away from the promoter DNA (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In the seven crystallographically independent copies of Tth CarD, the average distance between the α-carbons of CarD-RID-P13 and CarD-CTD-G100 is 5.7 ± 0.8 Å.
source: In the seven crystallographically independent copies of Tth CarD (PDB IDs 4L5G and structures reported here) (Srivastava et al., 2013), the average distance between the α-carbons of CarD-RID-P13 and CarD-CTD-G100 is 5.7 ± 0.8 Å, and among the four copies determined in the presence of promoter DNA, an even tighter distribution is observed, 5.2 ± 0.1 Å (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: Calculated from structural data reported here and in prior work (Srivastava et al., 2013).

claim: Among the four copies of Tth CarD determined in the presence of promoter DNA, the distance between the α-carbons of CarD-RID-P13 and CarD-CTD-G100 is 5.2 ± 0.1 Å.
source: In the seven crystallographically independent copies of Tth CarD (PDB IDs 4L5G and structures reported here) (Srivastava et al., 2013), the average distance between the α-carbons of CarD-RID-P13 and CarD-CTD-G100 is 5.7 ± 0.8 Å, and among the four copies determined in the presence of promoter DNA, an even tighter distribution is observed, 5.2 ± 0.1 Å (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: Calculated from structural data reported here.

claim: The corresponding positions in the Mtb CarD structure (P12/G99) are 24 Å apart.
source: On the other hand, the corresponding positions in the Mtb CarD structure (P12/G99) are 24 Å apart (Figure 4B, left) (Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Gulten and Sacchettini, 2013) and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cys substitutions at P12/G99 positions are predicted to form a disulfide bond under oxidizing conditions in the Tth CarD conformation.
source: Cys substitions at these positions are predicted to form a disulfide bond under oxidizing conditions in the Tth CarD conformation (thus locking the domain orientation), but not the Mtb CarD conformation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Predicted based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under oxidizing conditions, the CarD-RID and CarD-CTD were disulfide crosslinked in greater than 98% of CarD2C.
source: Non-reducing SDS polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and liquid chromatography mass spectrometry confirmed that under oxidizing conditions, the CarD-RID and CarD-CTD were disulfide crosslinked in greater than 98% of CarD2C, while under reducing conditions, no disulfide bond was present in >99% of CarD2C (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE and LC-MS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Under reducing conditions, no disulfide bond was present in greater than 99% of CarD2C.
source: Non-reducing SDS polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and liquid chromatography mass spectrometry confirmed that under oxidizing conditions, the CarD-RID and CarD-CTD were disulfide crosslinked in greater than 98% of CarD2C, while under reducing conditions, no disulfide bond was present in >99% of CarD2C (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE and LC-MS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Under oxidizing conditions, the cross-linked, conformationally locked CarD2C activated transcription as well as wild type CarD.
source: Under oxidizing conditions, the cross-linked, conformationally locked CarD2C activated transcription as well as wild type CarD (Figure 4D, 0 mM dithiothreitol [DTT], Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by abortive transcription assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Under reducing conditions, CarD2C was somewhat impaired in transcription activation.
source: The observation that under reducing conditions, CarD2C was somewhat impaired in transcription activation (Figures 4D, 5 mM DTT) is explained by the fact that the CarD positions corresponding to Mtb CarD P13 and G99 are conserved (Srivastava et al., 2013; Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Source code 1); on this basis substitution of these positions would be expected to impair uncrosslinked CarD2C function.
evidence: Supported by abortive transcription assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Tth CarD structures, with CarD-CTD W86 positioned to interact with the upstream edge of the transcription bubble, represents the functional conformation of CarD.
source: We conclude that the Tth CarD structures, with CarD-CTD W86 positioned to interact with the upstream edge of the transcription bubble (Figure 2), represents the functional conformation of CarD.
evidence: Concluded from the disulfide crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: CarD may stabilize RPo by forming favorable interactions with the upstream edge of the unwound transcription bubble.
source: CarD may stabilize RPo by forming favorable interactions with the upstream edge of the unwound transcription bubble (Figures 1C, 2B).
evidence: Inferred from structural data shown in Figures 1C and 2B.

claim: Tth CarD increased the half-life of the Thermus RPo approximately threefold on each promoter (23S and AP3).
source: Tth CarD increased the half-life (t1/2) of the Thermus RPo ∼threefold on each promoter (Figure 5B, Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) while Eco RNAP did not dissociate significantly from either promoter over the lifetime of the experiments (t1/2 >> 120 min; Figure 5B) (Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by half-life measurements shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Eco RNAP did not dissociate significantly from either promoter over the lifetime of the experiments (t1/2 >> 120 min).
source: Tth CarD increased the half-life (t1/2) of the Thermus RPo ∼threefold on each promoter (Figure 5B, Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) while Eco RNAP did not dissociate significantly from either promoter over the lifetime of the experiments (t1/2 >> 120 min; Figure 5B) (Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Tth CarD W86A substitution diminished or abolished the ability of CarD to increase t1/2 on the 23S and AP3 promoter, respectively.
source: The Tth CarD W86A substitution diminished or abolished the ability of CarD to increase t1/2 on the 23S and AP3 promoter, respectively (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by half-life measurements shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: On the duplex template (23S_DS), CarD increased the t1/2 more than fivefold.
source: On the duplex template (23S_DS), CarD increased the t1/2 more than fivefold (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: On the bubble template (23S_Bub) in the absence of CarD, the t1/2 was increased more than fivefold.
source: On the bubble template (Figure 6A, 23S_Bub) in the absence of CarD, the t1/2 was also increased more than fivefold, indicating that the relatively short lifetime of Tth RPo on the 23S promoter is due largely to bubble collapse (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The relatively short lifetime of Tth RPo on the 23S promoter is due largely to bubble collapse.
source: On the bubble template (Figure 6A, 23S_Bub) in the absence of CarD, the t1/2 was also increased more than fivefold, indicating that the relatively short lifetime of Tth RPo on the 23S promoter is due largely to bubble collapse (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of duplex and bubble template data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Addition of CarD to the bubble template had no effect on the level of transcription and did not affect RPo lifetime.
source: Addition of CarD to the bubble template had no effect on the level of transcription and did not affect RPo lifetime (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A primary function of Tth CarD is to stabilize RPo by preventing collapse of the transcription bubble.
source: We thus conclude that a primary function of Tth CarD, like Mtb CarD (Davis et al., 2015), is to stabilize RPo by preventing collapse of the transcription bubble.
evidence: Concluded from the bubble template experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Eco RNAP forms unusually stable RPo.
source: Eco has served as a model organism for the study of many cellular processes over the last few decades, including transcription. Eco RNAP forms unusually stable RPo and Eco lacks CarD, while RNAPs shown to form relatively unstable RPo come from bacteria that harbor CarD (Bacillus subtilis, Whipple and Sonenshein, 1992; Artsimovitch et al., 2000; Mtb, Davis et al., 2015; Myxococcus xanthus, Gallego-Garcia et al., 2014; Taq, Miropolskaya et al., 2012; Tth, Xue et al., 2000).
evidence: Cited from prior work and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: RNAPs shown to form relatively unstable RPo come from bacteria that harbor CarD.
source: Eco has served as a model organism for the study of many cellular processes over the last few decades, including transcription. Eco RNAP forms unusually stable RPo and Eco lacks CarD, while RNAPs shown to form relatively unstable RPo come from bacteria that harbor CarD (Bacillus subtilis, Whipple and Sonenshein, 1992; Artsimovitch et al., 2000; Mtb, Davis et al., 2015; Myxococcus xanthus, Gallego-Garcia et al., 2014; Taq, Miropolskaya et al., 2012; Tth, Xue et al., 2000).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Whipple and Sonenshein, 1992; Artsimovitch et al., 2000; Davis et al., 2015; Gallego-Garcia et al., 2014; Miropolskaya et al., 2012; Xue et al., 2000).

claim: CarD is a global regulator, found at most σA promoters throughout the Mycobacterium smegmatis genome.
source: Moreover, CarD is a global regulator, found at most σA promoters throughout the Mycobacterium smegmatis genome (Srivastava et al., 2013), and is essential in the two mycobacterial species where it has been tested (Stallings et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Srivastava et al., 2013).

claim: CarD is essential in the two mycobacterial species where it has been tested.
source: Moreover, CarD is a global regulator, found at most σA promoters throughout the Mycobacterium smegmatis genome (Srivastava et al., 2013), and is essential in the two mycobacterial species where it has been tested (Stallings et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Stallings et al., 2009).

claim: CarD boosts transcription at most (if not all) promoters by acting as a basal transcription factor, required to compensate for otherwise rapidly dissociating RNAP/promoter complexes.
source: These observations suggest that CarD boosts transcription at most (if not all) promoters by acting as a basal transcription factor, required to compensate for otherwise rapidly dissociating RNAP/promoter complexes.
evidence: Inferred from the observations about CarD distribution, essentiality, and function.

claim: T−12(t) is present at most σA promoters.
source: While the interaction with T−12(t) (Figure 2B, Figure 3B) may modulate the effect of CarD in a promoter-specific manner, this is likely to be a minor effect in vivo since T−12(t) is present at most σA promoters (Shultzaberger et al., 2007), and CarD can nevertheless activate transcription from promoters that lack a −12 T/A base pair (although less effectively; Figure 3B).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Shultzaberger et al., 2007).

claim: CarD can activate transcription from promoters that lack a −12 T/A base pair (although less effectively).
source: While the interaction with T−12(t) (Figure 2B, Figure 3B) may modulate the effect of CarD in a promoter-specific manner, this is likely to be a minor effect in vivo since T−12(t) is present at most σA promoters (Shultzaberger et al., 2007), and CarD can nevertheless activate transcription from promoters that lack a −12 T/A base pair (although less effectively; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CarD-RID/RNAP β1-lobe protein/protein interaction positions the CarD-CTD to interact with the upstream edge of the transcription bubble in a functionally relevant pose that does not allosterically alter the structure of the transcription bubble nor RNAP holoenzyme/promoter interactions.
source: The CarD-RID/RNAP β1-lobe protein/protein interaction positions the CarD-CTD to interact with the upstream edge of the transcription bubble in a functionally relevant pose that does not allosterically alter the structure of the transcription bubble nor RNAP holoenzyme/promoter interactions (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 6); instead CarD supports pre-existing RNAP holoenzyme/promoter DNA interactions in RPo.
evidence: Supported by structural and biochemical data shown in Figures 1D and 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The mode of CarD/DNA interaction is incompatible with duplex B-form DNA.
source: The mode of CarD/DNA interaction is incompatible with duplex B-form DNA; the normal minor groove is too narrow to accommodate the end of CarD-α3 and CarD-W86 (Srivastava et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Srivastava et al., 2013) and supported by structural analysis.

claim: A kinetic analysis of CarD function concluded CarD stabilizes RPo by increasing the rate of isomerization to RPo and decreasing the rate of bubble collapse.
source: This is consistent with a kinetic analysis of CarD function that concluded CarD stabilizes RPo by increasing the rate of isomerization to RPo and decreasing the rate of bubble collapse, but has little effect on the formation of the closed RNAP/promoter complex (Rammohan et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Rammohan et al., 2015).

claim: CarD has little effect on the formation of the closed RNAP/promoter complex.
source: This is consistent with a kinetic analysis of CarD function that concluded CarD stabilizes RPo by increasing the rate of isomerization to RPo and decreasing the rate of bubble collapse, but has little effect on the formation of the closed RNAP/promoter complex (Rammohan et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Rammohan et al., 2015).

claim: The CarD contacts with the DNA occur mostly through the backbone phosphates, except for highly conserved CarD-W86.
source: The CarD contacts with the DNA occur mostly through the backbone phosphates, except for highly conserved CarD-W86, which wedges between the splayed DNA strands at the upstream edge of the transcription bubble and may form a hydrogen bond with T−12(t) O2 presented in the highly distorted minor groove (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CarD-W86 wedges between the splayed DNA strands at the upstream edge of the transcription bubble and may form a hydrogen bond with T−12(t) O2 presented in the highly distorted minor groove.

evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The minor groove W-wedge increases the lifetime of RPo by preventing transcription bubble collapse.
source: The minor groove W-wedge increases the lifetime of RPo by preventing transcription bubble collapse (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: This previously unseen mode of transcription activation may be absent in Eco since Eco RNAP forms relatively stable complexes on most promoters.
source: This previously unseen mode of transcription activation may be absent in Eco (the focus of most mechanistic transcription studies) since Eco RNAP forms relatively stable complexes on most promoters (Figure 5B) (Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the data shown in Figure 5B and cited from prior work (Davis et al., 2015).

claim: Crystals of CarD transcription activation complexes were prepared by soaking Tth CarD into Taq Δ1.1σA-holoenzyme/us-fork (−12 bp) or full RPo crystals.
source: Crystals of CarD transcription activation complexes were prepared by soaking Tth CarD into Taq Δ1.1σA-holoenzyme/us-fork (−12 bp) or full RPo crystals (Bae et al., 2015).
evidence: Described as experimental method.

claim: Analysis of the diffraction data indicated high occupancy of one CarD molecule bound to each of two RNAP/promoter complexes in the asymmetric unit of the crystal lattice.
source: Analysis of the diffraction data indicated high occupancy of one CarD molecule bound to each of two RNAP/promoter complexes in the asymmetric unit of the crystal lattice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Reported as experimental result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The structures of CarD transcription activation complexes were refined to 4.4 and 4.3 Å-resolution, respectively.
source: The structures of CarD transcription activation complexes were refined to 4.4 and 4.3 Å-resolution, respectively (Table 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Reported as experimental result with crystallographic statistics in Table 2.

claim: The protein/protein and protein/nucleic acid interactions were essentially identical among all of the four crystallographically independent complexes.
source: The protein/protein and protein/nucleic acid interactions were essentially identical among all of the four crystallographically independent complexes, so the more complete and higher resolution CarD/RPo structure (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Table 2) is described here.
evidence: Reported as experimental observation.

claim: The architecture and interactions observed in the CarD/RPo structure are unlikely to be influenced by crystal packing interactions and likely represent the functional activation complex in solution.
source: Although the CarD bound to one RPo in the crystallographic asymmetric unit made crystal-packing interactions with a symmetry-related CarD, the CarD bound to the second RPo did not participate in any crystal-packing interactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating the architecture and interactions observed here are unlikely to be influenced by crystal packing interactions and likely represent the functional activation complex in solution.
evidence: Inferred from crystallographic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
